items.prompt: Which term describes an organism that makes its own organic compounds, such as a plant using photosynthesis?

options.label: Scavenger
Producer
Decomposer
Primary consumer

rubric: Producers (autotrophs) build their own organic compounds from light or chemical energy.
Decomposers and consumers get energy by feeding on other organisms or dead matter.

items.prompt: About what percentage of energy is usually passed from one trophic level to the next in a food chain?

options.label: About 90%
About 50%
About 100%
About 10%

rubric: The 10% rule is the standard approximation for energy transfer between trophic levels.
Higher figures ignore energy lost as heat and in waste.

items.prompt: What does the term 'carrying capacity' mean in ecology?

options.label: The maximum population size an environment can support
The highest rate at which a population can grow in ideal conditions
The number of different species living together in a community
The total mass of living material in the lowest trophic level

rubric: Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can sustain with its resources.
Other options confuse it with species richness, growth rate or biomass.

items.prompt: Which gas do plants take in from the air to use in photosynthesis?

options.label: Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Methane
Oxygen

rubric: Plants fix carbon dioxide into sugars during photosynthesis.
Oxygen is a product, and nitrogen is not taken up directly from air by most plants.

items.prompt: In ecology, what is a 'community'?

options.label: The specific place where an organism normally lives
All populations of different species living in the same area
All living and nonliving parts of an area together
All individuals of one species living in an area

rubric: A community is the set of interacting populations of different species in one area.
Distractors describe a population, an ecosystem and a habitat.

items.prompt: Which of the following are abiotic (nonliving) factors in an ecosystem? Select all that apply.

options.label: Air temperature
Annual rainfall
Soil pH
Predators
Fungi

rubric: Soil pH, temperature and rainfall are physical or chemical, nonliving factors.
Predators and fungi are living organisms, so they are biotic.

items.prompt: A student draws this food chain from a meadow: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. The teacher asks the student to name the secondary consumer, meaning the organism that eats the primary consumer. Which organism is it?

options.label: Snake
Frog
Grass
Grasshopper

rubric: The grasshopper is the primary consumer, so the frog that eats it is the secondary consumer.
The snake is the tertiary consumer; grass is the producer.

items.prompt: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?

options.label: Plants cannot produce enough food to support more than five different kinds of animals
Energy is lost as heat at each level, leaving too little at the top
Large predators at the top need so much territory that there is no space left for more levels
Decomposers remove most organisms before they can be eaten by higher levels

rubric: Most energy is lost through respiration as heat at each transfer, so little remains for top levels.
Other options give causes that do not explain the energy limit.

items.prompt: In a stable grassland, disease suddenly kills many of the foxes that eat rabbits. What is the most likely short-term effect on the rabbit population?

options.label: It will stay the same because food webs always balance
It will increase because fewer rabbits are being eaten
It will decrease because foxes help rabbits find food
It will disappear because rabbits depend on foxes to survive

rubric: Removing a predator reduces predation, so prey numbers usually rise at first.
Distractors assume prey depend on predators or that ecosystems never change.

items.prompt: A tick attaches to a deer and feeds on its blood, harming the deer but not usually killing it quickly. How is this relationship classified?

options.label: Parasitism
Commensalism
Mutualism
Competition

rubric: In parasitism one organism benefits while harming its host.
Mutualism benefits both, commensalism does not harm, and competition is between users of the same resource.

items.prompt: What is the role of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the nitrogen cycle?

options.label: They convert nitrogen into sugars using sunlight
They turn nitrogen gas into forms that plants can absorb
They absorb nitrates from soil and lock them away in rocks for millions of years
They release nitrogen gas back into the air by breaking down dead leaves

rubric: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric N2 into ammonia and related compounds usable by plants.
Other options mix up denitrification, sedimentary storage and photosynthesis.

items.prompt: An energy pyramid for a lake is widest at the bottom with producers. What does this wide base show?

options.label: Producers pass nearly all of their energy up to the top predators
Producers have the shortest lifespans of all the organisms
Producers hold the most energy, and less passes up each level
Producers are the largest organisms by body size in the lake

rubric: The base is widest because it holds the most energy, and less is passed up at each level.
Distractors confuse energy with body size, full transfer or lifespan.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain how decomposers help an ecosystem function? Select all that apply.

options.label: They break down waste so producers can reuse its elements
They add new energy to replace what is lost as heat
They release nutrients from dead matter back into the soil
They convert sunlight into chemical energy for the ecosystem

rubric: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter and waste for producers to reuse.
They do not capture sunlight or create new energy; energy flows one way and is lost as heat.

items.prompt: Fertiliser runs off a farm into a pond. Within weeks, algae cover the surface, and later many fish die even though no toxic chemical was found. A student wants to explain why the fish died. Which explanation best fits what happened?

options.label: Microbes breaking down the dead algae used up the oxygen in the water
The fish ate too many algae and could not digest the extra nutrients they contained
The surface algae raised the water temperature by absorbing nearly all the sunlight
The algae directly poisoned the fish by releasing fertiliser into the water

rubric: Extra nutrients cause an algal bloom; when algae die, decomposers use up dissolved oxygen, and fish suffocate.
Distractors invent poisoning, digestion problems or heating as the main cause.

items.prompt: Why do most food chains have only four or five trophic levels?

options.label: Much energy is lost as heat at each transfer, so too little remains to support more levels
Top consumers grow so large that the ecosystem cannot physically hold another level
Predators at higher levels refuse to eat animals that are too small to be worth hunting
Nutrients are used up by the lower levels, so none are left for top consumers

rubric: Energy is lost mainly as heat through respiration at each transfer, limiting chain length.
Distractors confuse energy flow with nutrient supply or with animal behaviour and size.

items.prompt: A tick feeds on the blood of a deer, harming the deer while the tick benefits. How is this relationship classified?

options.label: Competition
Mutualism
Commensalism
Parasitism

rubric: One species benefits at the host's expense, which is parasitism.
Mutualism and commensalism wrongly assume no harm to the host.

items.prompt: What does the carrying capacity of an environment describe?

options.label: The largest population size the environment can sustain over time with its available resources
The average number of offspring that each individual produces during its lifetime
The fastest rate at which a population can grow when resources are unlimited and space is free
The total number of different species that can live together in the same habitat

rubric: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum sustainable population given resources.
Distractors describe the intrinsic growth rate, species richness and fecundity.

items.prompt: What is the main role of decomposers in nutrient cycling?

options.label: They capture sunlight and turn it into chemical energy for the food web
They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil or water for producers to reuse
They remove nutrients from the ecosystem so that they cannot build up to harmful levels
They hunt weak animals so that nutrients move up to higher trophic levels

rubric: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead material back to the abiotic pool.
Distractors confuse decomposers with producers, predators or nutrient removal.

items.prompt: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk, which trophic level does the snake occupy?

options.label: Tertiary consumer
Quaternary consumer
Secondary consumer
Primary consumer

rubric: Grasshopper is primary, frog secondary, snake tertiary.
Other options come from miscounting, such as counting grass as a level or skipping one.

items.prompt: Which of the following are abiotic factors in a pond ecosystem? Select all that apply.

options.label: Density of algae
Light penetration
Number of frog species
Water temperature
Dissolved oxygen concentration

rubric: Temperature, dissolved oxygen and light are non-living physical or chemical factors.
Frog species and algae are living organisms, so they are biotic.

items.prompt: Fertilizer runoff from nearby farms enters a small lake. Within weeks the surface is covered in algae, and later many fish are found dead. A student wants to explain the fish deaths. Which explanation is best?

options.label: Dead algae were decomposed by bacteria, which used up the dissolved oxygen
The extra nutrients from the fertilizer poisoned the fish directly when they swallowed the contaminated water
The algae released so much extra oxygen that the water became toxic to the fish's gills over time
A thick algal mat blocked all the sunlight, so fish could no longer see well enough to find food

rubric: Eutrophication leads to algal die-off, and bacterial decomposition depletes oxygen.
Distractors suggest direct poisoning, vision problems or oxygen excess.

items.prompt: Producers in a meadow fix 10,000 kJ of energy. Using the 10% rule, how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

options.label: 100 kJ
10 kJ

rubric: Producers 10,000 → primary 1,000 → secondary 100 kJ.
1,000 kJ results from applying the rule only once.

items.prompt: A population of 1,000 mice has 120 births and 40 deaths in a year, with no immigration or emigration. What is the annual growth rate?
rubric: 12% ignores deaths; other values are arithmetic slips.

items.prompt: Researchers mark 50 turtles and release them. Later they catch 40 turtles, of which 10 are marked. Using the mark-recapture formula, what is the estimated population?
rubric: Other values come from dividing or combining the numbers incorrectly.

items.prompt: In a pond, frogs eat insects and herons eat frogs. A disease removes most of the frogs. What is the most likely short-term effect on the insects?

options.label: Insect numbers will fall because herons will switch to eating them
Insect numbers will increase because fewer insects are eaten
Insect numbers will stay the same because herons do not eat insects
Insect numbers will fall because the frogs' waste fed the insects

rubric: Removing a predator generally releases its prey from predation pressure.
Distractors assume prey switching or dependence that is not stated.

items.prompt: In the nitrogen cycle, ammonium in the soil is next converted by nitrifying bacteria into which compounds?

options.label: Ammonia gas, which is then released from the soil
Nitrite and then nitrate, which plants can take up
Nitrogen gas, which then escapes to the atmosphere
Amino acids, which are then used directly by plants

rubric: Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrite and then to nitrate.
Nitrogen gas is produced by denitrification, a different step.

items.prompt: A forest supports a deer population at its carrying capacity. Which changes would be expected to raise that carrying capacity? Select all that apply.

options.label: Winter snowfall increases and buries all forage
Part of the forest is cleared for housing
A severe multi-year drought reduces plant growth
A reliable new stream provides year-round water
Farmers plant new meadows of forage beside the forest

rubric: More food and water raise the number of deer the area can support.
Drought, habitat loss and buried forage reduce resources and lower carrying capacity.

items.prompt: A lake is contaminated with a persistent pesticide that is not excreted by organisms. The food chain is plankton → minnows → trout → ospreys. Using what you know about biomagnification, which organism will most likely carry the highest pesticide concentration in its tissues?

options.label: Trout, because they are the most numerous predators in the lake and eat minnows
Plankton, because they absorb it directly from the water in the largest amounts
Minnows, because they eat huge amounts of plankton and are the first consumers
Ospreys, because the pesticide builds up at each higher trophic level

rubric: Persistent toxins concentrate at each step, so top predators carry the most.
Distractors pick lower levels, ignoring accumulation up the chain.

items.prompt: A grassland producer level fixes 20,000 kJ/m^2/yr of energy. Assuming 10% transfer efficiency between trophic levels, how much energy reaches secondary consumers (the third trophic level)?

options.label: 200 kJ/m^2/yr
20 kJ/m^2/yr

rubric: Producers to primary consumers gives 2,000, then to secondary consumers gives 200.
Choosing 2,000 applies the 10% step only once.

items.prompt: A beetle population of 50 grows with a constant finite growth rate (lambda) of 1.2 per generation and no limits. What is the expected population after 2 generations?
rubric: Distractors add increments linearly instead of compounding.

items.prompt: In a mark-recapture study, 60 fish were marked and released. A later sample of 80 fish contained 12 marked fish. Using the Lincoln-Petersen estimate, what is the estimated population size?
rubric: N = (marked x second sample) / recaptured = 60 x 80 / 12 = 400.
16 comes from inverting the ratio.

items.prompt: A community has 4 species with 50, 30, 10 and 10 individuals (100 total). Using Simpson's index of diversity, 1 - sum(p^2), what is the value?
rubric: 0.36 is the dominance sum, not the diversity index.

items.prompt: A population follows logistic growth, dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K), with r = 0.5 per year and K = 1,000. What is the growth rate (individuals per year) when N = 200?
rubric: 100 ignores the density-dependent term.

items.prompt: Runoff carrying heavy fertilizer enters a small, still pond. Applying the usual sequence of eutrophication, which outcomes would you predict? Select all that apply.

options.label: Dissolved oxygen falls as dead algae decompose
Water clarity improves as nutrients are used up
Light reaching submerged plants decreases
Deep-water oxygen rises because of extra algal biomass
Algal blooms increase at the surface

rubric: Nutrients cause blooms, shading, then oxygen-consuming decomposition.
Clarity and oxygen increases contradict the sequence.

items.prompt: A student estimates the number of wildflowers in a 2,000 m^2 meadow. She places four randomly located 1 m^2 quadrats and counts 3, 5, 4 and 8 plants. She wants to scale the sample to the whole meadow. What is the best estimate of the population?

options.label: 20 plants
10,000 plants
2,000 plants
40,000 plants

rubric: Mean density is 5 per m^2, and 5 x 2,000 = 10,000.
40,000 uses the total count instead of the mean density.

items.prompt: Records show lynx numbers peaking one to two years after snowshoe hare peaks, then both crashing. Which interpretation best fits this pattern?

options.label: Hare numbers are set only by weather, and lynx simply track the climate
Lynx abundance is independent of hares because lynx numbers lag behind
Lynx respond to prey abundance with a delay, so predation can drive coupled cycles
Lynx and hares compete for the same food, so each limits the other directly

rubric: A lagged numerical response of predator to prey can generate coupled cycles.
A lag does not mean independence, and the two do not compete.

items.prompt: Two populations of equal size are compared. Population A is mostly pre-reproductive individuals; Population B is mostly post-reproductive individuals. Survival and fecundity are otherwise similar. Which analysis is most sound?

options.label: A is likely to grow, as many individuals will soon enter reproductive ages
Both will stay stable because their sizes are equal
B will grow faster because older individuals have survived longest
A is likely to decline because juveniles do not yet contribute births

rubric: Age structure with many pre-reproductive individuals predicts future growth.
Equal current size says nothing about future trajectory.

items.prompt: A mature forest has high gross primary productivity but its net primary productivity is low. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Decomposers consume most of the leaf litter the trees drop
Stomata close, so plants cannot absorb enough carbon dioxide
Shaded lower leaves fix less carbon than the canopy leaves
Plant respiration uses a large share of the carbon fixed

rubric: NPP = GPP minus producer respiration; large biomass has high respiratory costs.
Decomposer activity is not part of the NPP calculation.

items.prompt: On a rocky shore, barnacle species A lives only in the upper zone. When competitor species B is removed from the lower zone, A also colonises the lower zone and survives. What does this show?

options.label: Competition from B restricts A's realised niche
A is physically unable to tolerate the lower zone's conditions while B is present
B facilitates A by providing shelter from wave action in the upper zone
The upper zone is A's fundamental niche, so its range cannot expand

rubric: Expansion after competitor removal shows the realised niche was smaller than the fundamental niche.
The other options ignore the removal result.

items.prompt: A fertilised field is waterlogged for two weeks. Soil nitrate drops sharply and a little nitrous oxide is detected, though plants took up little nitrogen. What best explains this?

options.label: Nitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to ammonium in oxygen-rich soil pockets
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria take up nitrate to build nitrogen-rich root nodules
Denitrifying bacteria use nitrate in low-oxygen soil, releasing nitrogen gases
Nitrate is lost from the wet soil surface as ammonia gas through volatilisation

rubric: Waterlogging creates anaerobic conditions that favour denitrification.
Nitrification needs oxygen and produces nitrate rather than removing it.

items.prompt: Which observations would support the conclusion that a population is regulated by density-dependent factors? Select all that apply.

options.label: Per capita birth rate falls as density rises
A hurricane kills about 40% of individuals regardless of density
An early frost removes a fixed share of seedlings every year
Disease mortality rises in years when density is high

rubric: Density-dependent factors change per capita rates with density.
Storms and frost act independently of density.

items.prompt: Managers stock a fishless pond with predatory fish. Within months, zooplankton numbers drop and the water turns green with algae. Nutrient levels and temperature have not changed. Which analysis best explains the algal increase?

options.label: Fish eat algae directly and algae rebound in response
Fish consumed zooplankton, reducing grazing pressure on algae
Zooplankton competed with fish, so removing them boosted algae
Fish excretion lowered nutrient levels, favouring algae

rubric: A trophic cascade: predators reduce grazers, releasing algae from top-down control.
The other options contradict the observed unchanged nutrients or the feeding relationships.

items.prompt: After bass (which eat minnows) were removed from a lake, minnows boomed, zooplankton fell sharply, and phytoplankton rose. Which explanation best accounts for the rise in phytoplankton?

options.label: Reduced predation on phytoplankton let them evolve faster growth, raising their abundance within one season
Minnows began grazing phytoplankton directly, since they replaced bass as the dominant consumer in the lake
Bass had competed with phytoplankton for dissolved nutrients, so removing them freed nutrients for algal growth
Fewer bass let minnows cut zooplankton grazing, releasing phytoplankton from top-down control

rubric: A top-down cascade: more minnows, fewer zooplankton, less grazing on phytoplankton.
Distractors invent direct feeding, bass-algae competition, or rapid evolution, none of which fit the trophic chain.

items.prompt: In a logistic beetle population, the per-capita growth rate falls linearly from 0.8 at very low density to 0 at N = 500. At which population size is the total (absolute) growth rate greatest?
rubric: Total growth = rN(1 - N/K) peaks at K/2 = 250.
Choosing 500 confuses where per-capita rate is zero with maximum growth; choosing 125 or 400 has no basis in the curve.

items.prompt: A grassland produces 10,000 kJ/m2/yr of net primary production. Herbivore production is 900 kJ/m2/yr and carnivore production is 80 kJ/m2/yr. Which interpretation of these data is best supported?

options.label: Herbivores capture about 90% of plant production, and carnivores capture about 9% of what remains
Efficiency collapses at the carnivore step, so carnivores must assimilate far less of what they eat than herbivores do
Only 10% of energy is lost at each step, so about 90% of the energy passes up to the next level
Production passes up at about 9% at both steps, so the pyramid narrows by a roughly constant ratio

rubric: 900/10000 = 9% and 80/900 = about 8.9%, so transfer is similar at both steps.
Distractors reverse the loss and transfer percentages or read a drop in efficiency that the numbers do not show.

items.prompt: A Lincoln-Petersen mark-recapture estimate of population size is calculated. Which violated assumption would cause the estimate to be too HIGH rather than too low?

options.label: Observers sometimes mistake unmarked animals for marked ones when recording the second sample
Marked animals become trap-happy, so more of them are caught again than their share of the population predicts
Marked animals are released near the traps and resampled there, so they are over-represented in the second sample
Marked animals become trap-shy, so fewer of them are recaptured than their share of the population predicts

rubric: Fewer recaptures than expected means a smaller marked fraction, which inflates the estimate N = (M x C)/R.
The other options all raise the recapture count and so lower the estimate.

items.prompt: Stream nitrate concentration rose sharply for several years after a forested catchment was clear-cut. Which mechanism best explains the increase?

options.label: Plant uptake stopped while microbes kept mineralising and nitrifying nitrogen, so unused nitrate leached out
Atmospheric nitrogen deposition increased on the cleared area because fewer trees were present to intercept it, adding nitrate directly
Decomposition slowed after cutting, so nitrate built up in the litter layer and was then released by later heavy rainfall
Denitrification rose in the warmer, wetter exposed soil, converting nitrogen gas into nitrate that then washed into streams

rubric: Loss of plant uptake with continuing mineralisation and nitrification leaves excess mobile nitrate that leaches.
Denitrification removes nitrate, and slower decomposition or deposition changes do not explain a sharp multi-year rise.

items.prompt: On an intertidal shore the barnacle Chthamalus lives only in the upper zone. When Balanus, which dominates the lower zone, is removed, Chthamalus survives well in the lower zone too. Balanus transplanted to the upper zone dies from desiccation. Which conclusions are supported? Select all that apply.

options.label: Chthamalus's realized niche is narrower than its fundamental niche because of competition from Balanus
Chthamalus is physiologically unable to survive in the lower zone under any conditions
Chthamalus's upper limit on the shore is set mainly by competition from Balanus
Balanus's upper limit is set mainly by physical stress rather than by competition

rubric: Removal shows competition restricts Chthamalus below, and Balanus dying above shows physical stress limits it.
Distractors misplace competition at the upper limit or deny the removal result.

items.prompt: A surveyor records two grassland plots of 100 plants each. Plot A has 10 species: one with 91 individuals and nine with 1 each. Plot B has 10 species with 10 individuals each. A colleague says the plots are equally diverse because richness is identical. Which response is most accurate?

options.label: Plot A is more diverse, since each of its nine rare species counts heavily in the index and signals a richer community overall
Both plots are equally diverse, since indices like Shannon depend only on how many species are present, not on abundances
Plot A is more diverse, since a strongly dominant species indicates a productive and stable community with high diversity
Plot B is more diverse by indices that include evenness, since richness matches but Plot A is dominated by one species

rubric: Diversity indices combine richness and evenness, and Plot B is far more even.
Distractors treat richness alone as diversity or treat dominance or rarity as raising diversity.

items.prompt: A team must estimate the density of a rare, elusive, wide-ranging carnivore over 2,000 km2. Criteria: no handling of animals, individuals identifiable from natural markings, and an estimate that accounts for animal movement. Which method best meets these criteria?

options.label: Transect counts of visible animals, extrapolated by the proportion of the area sampled
Live-trapping with ear tags and a Lincoln-Petersen estimate, since marking gives direct recapture data
Counting tracks along roads as an index, then scaling the index to the whole area surveyed
Camera traps analysed with spatial capture-recapture models, using natural coat patterns and trap locations

rubric: Camera traps need no handling, identify individuals by markings, and spatial models account for movement.
Live-trapping violates the no-handling criterion; track and transect indices neither identify individuals nor model movement.

items.prompt: A weed invades a wetland that holds native relatives of the weed. Criteria: minimise risk to non-target species, even if control is slower. Which biological control agent is best?

options.label: A generalist herbivorous insect that feeds on many plants and therefore establishes and spreads quickly
A specialist on the weed's genus, tested only on the weed itself, since specialists rarely switch hosts
A specialist insect that, in host-range trials including native relatives, fed and reproduced only on the weed
A generalist fish that eats aquatic vegetation, since it can be removed later if it harms native plants

rubric: Host-range trials that include native relatives best demonstrate low non-target risk.
Generalists and untested specialists fail the non-target criterion; relatives may be attacked if never tested.

items.prompt: A report claims 'more species always makes an ecosystem more stable.' Judged against ecological evidence, which critique is strongest?

options.label: Diversity can stabilise total community biomass through asynchronous species responses, though individual populations may fluctuate more
Diversity stabilises communities mainly when added species share one trophic level, because competition among them then buffers biomass losses
Stability is largely unrelated to diversity, because experiments show community biomass varies about equally across species-rich and species-poor plots
The claim holds, because each added species contributes a roughly fixed amount of resistance to disturbance, so stability rises steadily with richness

rubric: Insurance and asynchrony effects stabilise aggregate properties, while individual populations can be more variable, so the claim is too broad.
Distractors deny any relationship, impose a false trophic restriction, or accept an unsupported additive rule.

items.prompt: A shallow lake has recurring cyanobacterial blooms. Phosphorus is limiting and comes mostly from farm runoff. Criteria: effect lasting for decades, and addressing the cause rather than the symptoms. Which intervention is best?

options.label: Apply algaecide each spring, since it removes blooms quickly and cheaply before they affect water use
Cut external phosphorus loading with catchment buffer strips and reduced fertilizer use on farms
Stock planktivorous fish to raise grazing, since that adds a living control on algal numbers
Aerate the lake bottom continuously, since that limits phosphorus release from sediments into the water

rubric: Reducing external phosphorus addresses the limiting nutrient at its source and lasts.
Algaecide and aeration treat symptoms, and stocking planktivores reduces zooplankton grazing.

items.prompt: Planners can protect 400 ha of forest for a bird community. Criteria: edge-sensitive species, large territories, and poor dispersal across farmland. Which reserve design best meets these criteria?

options.label: Eight scattered 50 ha fragments, to spread the risk of a local catastrophe such as fire or disease across many sites
Four 100 ha fragments separated by farmland, to capture a wider range of habitat types and support more species
One contiguous 400 ha block, which minimises edge and fits large territories without crossing farmland
A long, thin 400 ha strip along a river, to give every species maximum access to water and a continuous movement route

rubric: A single compact block reduces edge, supports large territories, and avoids dispersal across farmland.
Fragments and strips increase edge and isolation, which the stated species cannot tolerate.

items.prompt: A proposal would rate ecosystem health solely by net primary productivity (NPP). Which are valid criticisms? Select all that apply.

options.label: NPP cannot be estimated by any field or remote-sensing method, so it cannot be compared across sites
NPP equals standing biomass, so it adds no information beyond a simple count of trees
NPP can rise under nutrient enrichment while species richness and composition decline
NPP says nothing about whether species are native or whether key functions and interactions are intact

rubric: NPP can increase with eutrophication and ignores composition and function.
NPP is measurable and is a rate, not standing biomass; the other options misstate this.

items.prompt: A manager estimates a fish stock's carrying capacity at 100,000 t with logistic growth, so maximum sustainable yield occurs near a stock of 50,000 t. The estimate is highly uncertain, and earlier overestimates led to collapse. Criteria: sustain yield and avoid collapse. Which policy is best?

options.label: Close the fishery until carrying capacity is measured exactly, since any harvest under uncertainty risks collapse
Set quotas at the estimated MSY level, since it maximises yield and errors in the estimate are equally likely in both directions
Set quotas below the estimated MSY and adjust them as monitoring narrows the uncertainty
Keep the stock near estimated carrying capacity, since the largest population always gives the largest long-term harvest

rubric: A precautionary, adaptive quota keeps yield while buffering against overestimated capacity.
Harvesting at the estimated MSY ignores asymmetric collapse risk, yield is near zero at K, and a total closure sacrifices yield unnecessarily.

items.prompt: After wolf reintroduction in one park, elk numbers fell and willow stands recovered. A reviewer claims this proves top-down control operates in all terrestrial systems. Which critique of the claim is strongest?

options.label: One site cannot establish generality, because behavioural effects, climate and bottom-up productivity differ among systems.
Elk decline shows predators limit prey, but willows are producers, so no cascade can occur in any food web.
Willow recovery cannot reflect lower herbivory because plants respond only to soil nutrients and rainfall in every habitat.
Top-down control is impossible on land because energy limits predators to a few individuals, so the effect must be coincidence.

rubric: Generalising from a single system ignores context-dependence of trophic control.
Distractors wrongly deny top-down effects or cascades outright.

items.prompt: In a Lincoln-Petersen study, marked animals become trap-happy and enter traps more readily than unmarked ones. The estimate is N = (M x C) / R. What is the likely effect on the estimate?

options.label: It underestimates N, because recaptures R are inflated relative to a random sample of the population.
It overestimates N, because unmarked individuals avoid traps and so shrink the second sample C.
It is unbiased, because marking does not change M and the ratio of marked to total stays constant.
It overestimates N, because marked animals are over-counted in the second sample and inflate C.

rubric: Trap-happy behaviour raises R relative to random sampling, which lowers N.
Distractors misattribute the bias to C or assume the equal-catchability assumption still holds.

items.prompt: A manager argues that adding species always stabilises total community biomass. Which judgement best reflects the evidence on diversity and stability?

options.label: Stability rises with richness because every added species contributes equal biomass and so reduces variance.
Stability depends on asynchronous species responses that buffer total biomass, not simply on the number of species.
Random complex webs are always more stable, so richness alone determines stability in any community.
Species-poor communities are more stable because fewer links let disturbance spread, regardless of species' responses.

rubric: The insurance/portfolio effect depends on differing responses among species.
Distractors assume richness alone (or its absence) decides stability.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to decide whether herbivore biomass in grasslands is limited mainly from the bottom up or the top down. Which evidence is most diagnostic?

options.label: A positive correlation between plant and herbivore biomass across sites, which only bottom-up control can produce.
A fall in herbivore biomass during a drought year, which shows that predators regulate the herbivores.
A factorial experiment crossing predator exclusion with fertilisation, showing which treatment shifts herbivore biomass.
Higher predator counts at sites with many herbivores, which shows that predators are what limit herbivore numbers.

rubric: Only crossed manipulations separate the two controls and their interaction.
Correlations and single-year changes are compatible with either mechanism.

items.prompt: A lake is phosphorus-limited, suffers cyanobacterial blooms, and receives most phosphorus from agricultural runoff. Criteria: addresses the cause and keeps long-term cost low. Which option is best?

options.label: Seasonal copper sulfate dosing, because killing cyanobacteria as they appear removes the bloom problem at low cost.
Buffer strips and nutrient management in the catchment, because cutting phosphorus inputs tackles the limiting resource.
Nitrogen addition, because raising the N:P ratio favours green algae over cyanobacteria and ends the blooms.
Stocking planktivorous fish, because they add grazing pressure that suppresses algae throughout the season.

rubric: Reducing the limiting nutrient at its source treats the cause durably.
Planktivores reduce zooplankton grazers, and copper or nitrogen treat symptoms or worsen conditions.

items.prompt: A team compares two communities using only the Shannon diversity index. Which are valid limitations of this approach? Select all that apply.

options.label: It weights species by body mass automatically, so large species are counted properly.
It ignores species identity, so replacing one species with another changes nothing.
Its value depends on sampling effort, so unequal samples can bias comparisons.
Different mixes of richness and evenness can give the same value, hiding structural differences.
It captures functional roles, so it reliably detects loss of ecosystem function.

rubric: Shannon blends richness and evenness, is sample-size sensitive, and is blind to identity.
It does not include function or body mass.

items.prompt: A fishery agency sets its quota at the maximum sustainable yield from a logistic model (harvest at K/2). Recruitment varies strongly between years, and the biomass estimate carries about 30% uncertainty. A manager must judge this policy. Which assessment is best?

options.label: The quota should be raised, because variable recruitment means stocks recover quickly from any overharvest and the buffer is unnecessary.
Uncertainty is irrelevant to the quota, because the model's equilibrium behaviour holds when outcomes are averaged across many years.
The policy is risky, because overestimated biomass can drive overharvest; a lower harvest rate buffers the uncertainty.
The policy is safe, because logistic growth guarantees the stock returns to K/2 after any level of harvest, so quotas self-correct.

rubric: MSY targets with noisy estimates and variable recruitment raise collapse risk, which supports precaution.
Distractors treat deterministic equilibrium as guaranteed in a stochastic system.

items.prompt: You must test whether a bird predator limits grasshopper density in a meadow, while controlling for cage effects on microclimate. Which design meets both requirements?

options.label: Comparison of meadows that naturally have many versus few birds, since natural variation avoids cage artefacts altogether.
Randomised replicated plots with full exclosures, partial-cage controls and open plots, then compare grasshopper density.
Removal of birds from all plots, comparing before and after counts, since each plot then serves as its own control.
One fenced plot and one open plot, then compare final counts to show the effect of removing the birds.

rubric: Replicated exclosures with cage controls isolate predator effects from caging artefacts.
Distractors lack replication, randomisation or a concurrent control.

items.prompt: Design monitoring to estimate the trend in site occupancy of a secretive amphibian whose detection probability is below 1 and varies with weather. Which design meets this need?

options.label: One visit per site each year, treating sites where it is seen as occupied, because repeat visits add cost without new information.
Repeat visits per site within a season, recording weather, and an occupancy model that separates detection from occupancy.
Many visits only at sites where it was previously found, to maximise detections and so improve the occupancy estimate.
One visit in the best weather only, treating non-detections as absences since detection is then close to certain.

rubric: Repeat surveys with covariates let an occupancy model estimate detection separately from occupancy.
Distractors treat non-detection as absence or bias site selection.

items.prompt: A viability analysis for an isolated population of about 40 individuals uses only mean growth rate and carrying capacity. What is the most important element the model is missing?

options.label: Demographic and environmental stochasticity, plus possible Allee effects and inbreeding, which dominate risk at small sizes.
Average adult body mass, because it determines the growth rate and therefore sets extinction risk directly.
A larger carrying capacity, because deterministic models systematically underestimate the number a habitat can support.
Continental-scale mean rainfall, because climate averages fix extinction risk more than any population-level process does.

rubric: Small populations are governed by chance events and density-dependent costs, which means-based models omit.
Distractors add inputs that do not address small-population dynamics.

items.prompt: Forest A was sampled with 200 trapped individuals and forest B with 800. Design an analysis that compares species richness fairly.

options.label: Discard rare species so both samples contain only common ones, since rare species are mostly sampling noise.
Divide each species count by individuals sampled, since a per-individual rate removes any dependence on effort.
Rarefy or use coverage-based interpolation to a common sample size or completeness before comparing the forests.
Compare raw species counts, since the larger sample describes forest B more completely and so is more reliable.

rubric: Standardising sample size or coverage removes effort-driven differences in richness.
Raw counts and ratios confound effort with richness, and dropping rare species biases the comparison.

items.prompt: An island has invasive cats and rats, and both eat seabird chicks; cats also suppress rats. Goal: seabird recovery with no mesopredator release. Which plan meets this?

options.label: Remove only cats, since rats will then decline without any need for a separate campaign against them.
Remove only rats, since cats will then lose their prey and will leave the seabirds alone.
Coordinate removal of both cats and rats, with seabird and predator monitoring to catch any rebound.
Remove neither, and instead fence the colonies, since fencing guarantees recovery without altering predator numbers.

rubric: Removing both invaders avoids rat release and cat prey-switching onto seabirds.
Single-species removal can worsen seabird losses.

items.prompt: You design a mesocosm experiment to separate the effects of warming from those of nutrient enrichment on algal biomass. Which design features are required? Select all that apply.

options.label: A factorial crossing of temperature and nutrient levels, so main effects and interaction can be estimated.
One high-nutrient tank per temperature, to maximise the signal in each treatment.
An ambient-temperature, unfertilised control treatment as a baseline.
Warming all tanks and enriching only half, with no unmanipulated control treatment.
Replication of every treatment combination with randomised placement of tanks.

rubric: Crossed factors, replication with randomisation, and a baseline control are needed to separate the effects.
Unreplicated or confounded designs cannot isolate the two factors.

items.prompt: A planner can fund three reserves for a butterfly metapopulation. Constraints: each patch at least 50 ha, patches within 2 km of each other for dispersal, and no more than two reserves in the same flood-prone catchment. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: Three 80 ha patches 5 km apart in different catchments, giving large areas and flood independence.
Three 40 ha patches 1 km apart in different catchments, giving close spacing and flood independence.
Three 60 ha patches within 1.5 km of each other, split across two catchments with different flood exposure.
Three 70 ha patches 1 km apart, all in one floodplain catchment, giving large areas and close spacing.

rubric: Only this design satisfies size, dispersal distance and flood-spread constraints together.
Each distractor violates one constraint: dispersal, size or flood risk.
